finding: The claim-to-unit mapping is required everywhere and stored nowhere. §4.6.1 requires `cr review` to emit, per unit, "the claims mapped to it" — so `cr` must already hold the mapping before any role runs. But no schema holds it: the claim record of §3.3 has no unit field, the unit record of §3.4.6 has no claim field, and §2.3 lists no file for it. No command writes it: §4.1.1 ("Every unit MUST be mapped to zero or more claims") names no producer, and mapping is a judgement §2.1.3 does not delegate to `cr`. Everything downstream then fails: §10.2.3 ("Every claim is mapped to at least one unit") cannot be evaluated, and §4.1.3's unimplemented-claim entry, which "MUST be recorded in `coverage.ndjson`", has no writer either — `cr cells record` is the only writer of that file and §4.5.6 requires it to "reject with exit code 1 a cell naming an unknown unit id", while an unimplemented-claim entry has no unit id at all.
suggestion: Name the producer and the storage. Either add `claims` to the unit record of §3.4.6 and a `cr map record <pr> <file>` command that the agent feeds before `cr review`, or add a `units` array to the claim record written by `cr claims record`. Then either give §4.5.6 an explicit entry shape for a unit-less unimplemented-claim entry, or move those entries out of `coverage.ndjson` into a file §2.3 defines with its own writer.

finding: §5.4.3's gap ladder is declared "total over every run" but has no rung for an undetermined count, unlike §5.3.4 rung 4. Its fourth rung is "the failed count is zero → `passed`; otherwise → `failed`". `tests.count_pattern` is optional in §2.4 (Required = no), so on any profile that configures none — or whose pattern does not match — the failed count is never zero (it is unknown), and every gap probe falls through to `failed`. §5.4.4 then makes that `failed` result support a `probed` grade whenever the finding's `claim` field names the claim, and forces "Severity MUST be at least `high`". A suite that passed therefore manufactures a high-severity probed assertion. §5.5's per-kind table gives `gap` no `inconclusive` value, so an implementer cannot even record the honest outcome. §5.3.5 states the intent explicitly for mutations — "nor a runner whose output `cr` cannot parse ... can manufacture evidence" — and the gap ladder has no equivalent. Two engineers write opposite tests for "gap probe, no count_pattern, suite exits 0": `passed` (exit-code reading) vs `failed` (literal reading).
suggestion: Add an `inconclusive` rung to §5.4.3 between `no-tests-selected` and `passed` — "the executed or failed count is undetermined → `inconclusive`" — add `inconclusive` to the `gap` row of §5.5's per-kind table, and extend §5.4.5 to list `inconclusive` among the results that MUST NOT support a `probed` grade.

finding: §6.2.5's repair pins the match key too loosely to close the forgery it names. It says `cr` sets `origin: rule` only on a citation it generated, "matching the record's `rule` id against its own recorded hit in `rule-stats.ndjson`" — rule id alone. But §2.6.1.6 defines that store as carrying "the rule id, the round, and the head", with no path and no line, so a rule-id match cannot distinguish `cr`'s own hit location from an arbitrary location the agent supplied. Meanwhile `rule` is an ordinary agent-written field (§6.1: "| `rule` | no | The rule id, when a rule produced the record |"), not listed among the fields §6.1.4 forbids the agent to write. So an agent that stamps `rule: <any-rule-that-hit-this-round>` on a record and supplies a citation inside its own unit gets `origin: rule` computed onto it, which satisfies the §6.2 `cited` row ("that entry either has `origin: rule` or lies outside the record's own unit") and licenses the record to be posted as an assertion rather than forced to a question by §6.3.1. This is the same self-granted in-unit exemption §6.2.5 was written to close, reached through a different field.
suggestion: Make the match positional, not nominal. Extend §2.6.1.6 so every rule hit is appended to `rule-stats.ndjson` with the matched `path` and `line` alongside the rule id, round and head — §2.6.1.3 already has both at detection time. Then reword §6.2.5 to: `cr` MUST set `origin: rule` only on a citation whose `(rule id, path, line, head)` equals a hit `cr` itself recorded for the current round; every other citation MUST get `origin: agent`. Additionally mark `rule` computed in §6.1 (or require §6.1.4 to reject an agent-supplied `rule` that names no recorded hit for that record's unit), so the field cannot be used as a key into `cr`'s own evidence.

finding: §10.2.3 makes an unimplemented claim block "until it is either mapped, or set aside by a note per §3.6 naming it out of scope for this pull request". Nothing defines how `cr` establishes that a note names a claim out of scope. §3.6.1 gives a note only an id, text, timestamp, PR and source — there is no claim reference and no scope field — and §2.1.3 and §4.1.5 forbid `cr` from deciding this by text: "`cr` MUST NOT decide this by matching text." §4.1.5 supplies the missing machinery for the parallel unmapped-unit case (the agent decides, and "the coverage cell MUST cite the note id"), but §10.2 has no equivalent recorded decision and no command that writes one. Convergence condition 3 is therefore not mechanically evaluable, and this condition is the sole thing that makes an unimplemented claim block at all.
suggestion: Add an explicit recorded decision — e.g. `cr claims scope <pr> <claim-id> --out-of-scope --note <note-id>` — storing the note id against the claim, and rewrite §10.2.3 to block until the claim is mapped or carries such a recorded out-of-scope decision. `cr` then reads a field rather than judging prose.

finding: The profile schema has no field describing which paths are tests, yet two requirements depend on one. §5.4.2 defaults `probe.test_dir` to "the profile's first test glob root" — there is no test-glob field in the §2.4 table (`match.globs` is documented as "Source globs this profile owns"), so the stated default resolves against nothing. §4.4.1 likewise requires `cr` to "attach to every unit the test files changed or added by the PR", which needs a mechanical definition of a test file that no profile field, config key, or default supplies. Both are `cr`-side mechanical work, so §2.1 forbids deferring the decision to the agent.
suggestion: Add `tests.globs` (array, required when `tests.cmd` is present) to the §2.4 table, define it as the patterns that identify test files, and restate §5.4.2's default as "the root of the first entry in `tests.globs`" and §4.4.1's attachment as "changed files matching `tests.globs`".

finding: The profile schema row still reads "`tests.count_pattern` | string | no | Regex with one capture group yielding the executed test count", while §5.2.1 now requires the opposite: "`tests.count_pattern` MUST yield two capture groups, the executed count and the failed count". Profile validation is a §2.4 concern (§2.5.3: a malformed profile MUST abort with exit code 3), so an implementer cannot tell whether a one-group pattern is valid, and §5.3.4's rungs 3-5 and §5.4.3's rungs 3-4 all depend on a failed count that a one-group pattern can never yield.
suggestion: Rewrite the §2.4 row as "Regex with two capture groups: the executed count then the failed count", and state in §2.4 (or §5.2.1) that a pattern compiling to any other number of groups aborts with exit code 3, naming the profile.

finding: The profile table row still reads "`tests.count_pattern` | string | no | Regex with one capture group yielding the executed test count", but §5.2.1 — rewritten this round — says "`tests.count_pattern` MUST yield two capture groups, the executed count and the failed count". The whole result ladder of §5.3.4 and §5.4.3 depends on the failed count existing, so the §2.4 row is not merely stale prose: an implementer validating a profile against §2.4 would accept a one-group pattern and then have no failed count for rungs 5 and 6 of §5.3.4.
suggestion: Rewrite the §2.4 row as "Regex with two capture groups yielding the executed and failed test counts" and state that a pattern compiling to any other group count aborts with exit code 3 naming the profile, so the arity is validated at load rather than discovered at ladder-evaluation time.

finding: The §2.4 profile table defines `tests.count_pattern` as "Regex with one capture group yielding the executed test count", while §5.2.1 requires "`tests.count_pattern` MUST yield two capture groups, the executed count and the failed count". The whole of §5.3.4 depends on a failed count (rungs 4 and 5); an implementer who follows §2.4 can never derive `no-test-failed` and every mutation probe becomes `inconclusive`, killing the mutation axis. A tester cannot decide what a one-group pattern must do: load normally (§2.4) or abort (§5.2.1) — and §5.2.1 names no exit code for the violation either.
suggestion: Change the §2.4 row to "Regex with two capture groups yielding the executed and failed test counts", and state in §5.2.1 that a configured pattern whose compiled form has fewer than two capture groups MUST abort with exit code 3 naming the profile, so the failure is observable.

finding: §3.4.6 keys unit identity on position — an id is "reused across rounds for a unit whose file paths and hunk ranges are unchanged" — while §10.2.2 keys coverage invalidation on content: "A unit unchanged since an earlier round keeps its cells, so a delta round per §9.3.5 does not invalidate coverage it did not touch; a unit whose content changed needs its row filled again." The two criteria disagree in the most common push there is. Because §3.4.1 takes the diff "against the PR merge base at the current head", inserting a hunk near the top of a file shifts the hunk ranges of every later unit in that file. Their content is byte-identical and their unit hash unchanged, but their ranges changed, so they get fresh `u<n>` ids, and cells recorded against the old ids no longer belong to any unit in the current unit set. §10.2.2 then demands a complete row for units whose content nobody touched — exactly the invalidation §10.2.2 says a delta round must avoid.
suggestion: Key id reuse on the unit hash plus the file path set rather than on hunk ranges: a unit whose changed-line content and files are unchanged keeps its id even when its line numbers moved. Hunk ranges then become mutable attributes of the unit, and §10.2.2's content-based rule and §3.4.6's identity rule agree.

finding: §3.4.6 makes the unit `id` "reused across rounds for a unit whose file paths and hunk ranges are unchanged", but hunk ranges are line numbers: adding a line anywhere above a unit shifts its ranges without touching its content. Such a unit gets a new `u<n>`, so §10.2.2's "A unit unchanged since an earlier round keeps its cells, so a delta round per §9.3.5 does not invalidate coverage it did not touch" is false exactly in the case it was written for — the row of cells is keyed by unit id and the untouched unit now has none. Two engineers write opposite convergence tests for "push adds one line at the top of the file": one matches carried-over cells by unit id, the other by unit hash. §4.5.5 has cells carry both, so the text supports either reading, and §4.5.6 additionally rejects "a cell naming an unknown unit id", which strands the old cells.
suggestion: Key id reuse on the unit hash rather than on hunk ranges — "reused for a unit whose file paths and unit hash are unchanged" — or state in §10.2.2 that a cell satisfies the row when its `unit_hash` equals the current unit's hash regardless of the unit id it was recorded against.

finding: §4.1.3 requires that an unimplemented-claim entry "MUST be recorded in `coverage.ndjson` against the intent axis", but §4.5.5 defines the only record type that file holds and it cannot express one: "Every cell MUST carry the unit id and role id it sits at, one of `pass`, `finding`, `question`, or `na`, the head it was filled against, the unit hash of §3.4.6 it was filled for". An unimplemented claim has no unit "by construction" (§4.1.3's own words), so it has no unit id and no unit hash, and no cell field carries a claim id — yet §10.2.3 must block per claim. §4.5.6 then closes the only write path both ways: it "MUST reject with exit code 1 a cell naming an unknown unit id", and `cr` "MUST NOT invent a cell for a unit no role reported on", while the entry is mechanically derived by `cr`, not reported by a role.
suggestion: Give the unimplemented-claim entry its own record type and its own file (for example `intent-gaps.ndjson` in §2.3) with fields `claim`, `axis`, `round`, `head`, and a resolution field, and change §4.1.3, §10.1.2 and §10.2.3 to reference it. Leave `coverage.ndjson` to unit×role cells only.

finding: The two capture groups §5.2.1 now depends on contradict the profile schema that defines the field, and the fallout disables the only grade that may assert. §5.2.1 states "`tests.count_pattern` MUST yield two capture groups, the executed count and the failed count", while §2.4's profile table still defines "| `tests.count_pattern` | string | no | Regex with one capture group yielding the executed test count |". If §2.4 governs, the failed count is never derivable, and §5.3.4 rung 4 catches every mutation run — "the executed or failed count is undetermined ... → `inconclusive`" — while §5.3.5 rules that "`inconclusive` MUST NOT support a `probed` grade". §5.4.3's gap ladder depends on the same missing count for its "the failed count is zero → `passed`" rung. The result is that every probe runs the full suite in the sandbox under the §5.6.1 lock and the §5.6.4 cap, and none of them can ever raise a grade above `argued`. That is the exact ceremony this lens exists to catch: wall-clock and test-suite contention spent on experiments whose outcome cannot change what reaches the author, and it also removes the one escalation path §4.4.3 and §13.2 tell the agent to prefer over asserting.
suggestion: Update §2.4's row to match §5.2.1: "Regex with two capture groups yielding the executed and failed test counts". State explicitly what happens when a configured pattern yields only one group — either abort with exit code 3 naming the profile, consistent with §2.6.1.2's treatment of an uncompilable pattern, or define the second count as undetermined — so the shipped `laravel-pest` and `generic` profiles of §2.4.5 cannot silently reduce every probe to `inconclusive`.

finding: §5.3.5 states "Only `no-test-failed` proves the gap, and only when the filtered baseline of §5.2.2 passed", but a filter is optional: §5.5 marks `filter` Required = no and marks `baseline` "required for a filtered `mutation` probe", so an unfiltered mutation probe is legal and has no filtered baseline. Under the literal text its precondition can never be met, so an unfiltered mutation probe can never yield `probed`; under the obvious repair the unfiltered baseline of §5.2.2 sentence 1 substitutes. A tester writing "unfiltered mutation probe, suite passes with the mutation applied → is the finding gradable `probed`?" gets opposite answers, and the two answers differ in exactly the direction that matters for the trust economy.
suggestion: Restate §5.3.5 as "only when the baseline for this probe's filter — the filtered baseline of §5.2.2 for a filtered run, the unfiltered baseline for an unfiltered run — passed", and make `baseline` required for every mutation probe rather than only filtered ones.

finding: §5.3.4 gained rung 4 this round precisely to stop an unreadable run from proving anything — "the executed or failed count is undetermined, whether because no `tests.count_pattern` is configured or because the configured pattern did not match the output → `inconclusive`" — and §5.3.5 spells out the reason: no "runner whose output `cr` cannot parse" may manufacture evidence. §5.4.3's gap ladder has no such rung: "the failed count is zero → `passed`; otherwise → `failed`". Since §2.4 makes `tests.count_pattern` optional and §5.2.1 says a pattern that does not match "leaves both counts undetermined", an undetermined failed count is not zero and falls straight through to `failed`. On the shipped `generic` profile, every gap probe therefore returns `failed`, and §5.4.4 lets a `failed` gap probe support a `probed` grade at severity "at least `high`" whenever the record names a claim. A passing supplied test is reported to the author as proof the behaviour is broken.
suggestion: Add the same rung to §5.4.3 before the failed-count rungs — "the executed or failed count is undetermined → `inconclusive`" — add `inconclusive` to the `gap` row of §5.5's per-kind table, and add it to §5.4.5's list of results that "prove nothing and MUST NOT support a `probed` grade".

finding: §5.4.2 requires the probe test file to be placed "under `probe.test_dir` (default the profile's first test glob root) with a name derived from the probe id", and §5.1.6 defines a clean sandbox as one where there is "no file under `probe.test_dir` whose name matches the probe naming scheme of §5.4.2". Neither the directory default nor the naming scheme is determinable: §2.4 declares no test-glob field at all (its only glob fields are `match.globs` for source and `globs`/`exempt` on rules), so "the profile's first test glob root" points at a field that does not exist; and "a name derived from the probe id" is not a scheme. Both the exit-4 collision check of §5.4.2 and the leftover-artefact half of §5.1.6 — the mechanism that enforces the "probes revert" invariant — are therefore non-verifiable: two implementations write `p3.php` and `ProbeP3Test.php`, and neither detects the other's leftover.
suggestion: Add a `tests.globs` field to §2.4 (or name an explicit `probe.test_dir` default per shipped profile), and pin the file name to a literal template such as `cr_probe_<probe-id>.<ext>` with the extension taken from the profile, so both the collision check and the cleanliness scan are testable.

finding: §5.5's `baseline` row is "Id of the filtered baseline it was compared against, without which §5.3.5 cannot be evaluated", but no schema in the spec can produce that id. §5.5's `kind` is "`mutation` or `gap`" and `result` is "A value from the per-kind table below", neither of which describes a baseline run; §2.3 lists `probes.ndjson` for "Probe records (§5.5)" and no file for the test runs of §5.2; and §5.2.1 says only what `cr test` "MUST run ... and record", never where or under what id. The central grading gate of §5.3.5 therefore rests on a record a tester cannot construct, locate, or assert on, and "MUST be recorded once per head" (§5.2.2) has no observable outcome.
suggestion: Either give test runs their own schema and file (`runs.ndjson`, ids `r<n>`, with the fields of §5.2.1 plus `filter` and `head`) and make §5.5's `baseline` reference that id space, or add `baseline` as a third `kind` in §5.5 with its own result vocabulary.

finding: §6.2.5 says `cr` "MUST set `origin: rule` only on a citation it generated itself from its own detection pass of §2.6.1 ... and MUST set `origin: agent` on every citation the agent supplied". But §2.6.1.5 makes the agent the author of every rule-derived record — "Detection MUST report hits, never verdicts. The agent decides whether a hit is a real violation" — so the citation on that record was supplied by the agent and must be stamped `origin: agent`. That makes §2.6.1.3 unreachable: it promises that a hit "MUST be recorded as a `citations` entry per §6.1 carrying the matched `path`, `line`, and `origin: rule`, which grades the record `cited`". Under §6.2.5 no record an agent can write ever carries `origin: rule`, so a mechanical rule hit inside its own unit grades `argued` and is forced to a question — nullifying the entire mechanical-detection path to `cited` that §2.6 exists to provide. Nothing in the spec says `cr` injects a citation into an agent-authored record.
suggestion: Say explicitly that at record time `cr` matches each supplied citation's `(path, line)` and the record's `rule` id against its own recorded hits in `rule-stats.ndjson`, stamps `origin: rule` on the ones that match a hit it produced, and `origin: agent` on all others. That keeps `origin` computed and unforgeable while making §2.6.1.3 reachable.

finding: §8.1.5 states that "`cr` MUST refuse to post a `kind=question` body containing no `?` character, with exit code 1 naming the record id." §9.4.2 forces every reply record to `kind: question`, and §9.6.5 routes the withdrawal reply through that same shape. A withdrawal ("I am dropping this concern") is by construction not a question, so `cr post --confirm` will refuse the reply §9.6.5 mandates unless the agent inserts a cosmetic question mark — which is exactly the empty register §8.1.5 exists to prevent. §8.1.4's `cr`-owned label likewise names "the register and the grade" of a question, which misdescribes a withdrawal.
suggestion: Give withdrawal replies their own kind (for example `kind: withdrawal`) exempt from §8.1.5 and §8.1.4's question label, with its own built-in `cr`-owned label; or state explicitly in §8.1.5 that the check applies only to records with an `anchor`-anchored question and not to reply records created by §9.6.5.

finding: §8.1.7 restates the round-3 requirement without giving `cr` any mechanism or check to enforce it, so a `cited` assertion can still reach the author with its warrant stripped. §8.1.7 says "Every citation of a `cited` record MUST be rendered into the posted body as `path:line`", but the posted body is not `cr`'s to write: §7.1.2 says "The block body MUST be free-form Markdown that the user may rewrite entirely", and §8.1.2 mandates that the agent rewrite it — "The agent then rewrites that body in `render.lang` by editing `draft.md`" — while forbidding `cr` from touching it: "`cr` MUST NOT translate or compose, and MUST NOT accept a body through any other channel." The citations §6.2.6 renders into the initial draft block are therefore discarded by the mandatory rewrite, and nothing restores or checks them. Contrast the two places the spec solves this same problem properly: §8.1.4 makes the question label "a fixed, `cr`-owned label line" prepended outside the body and protected by §2.7, and §8.1.5 gives an explicit post-time refusal ("MUST refuse to post a `kind=question` body containing no `?` character, with exit code 1 naming the record id"). §8.1.7 has neither, so it is a requirement no component is obliged to satisfy.
suggestion: Give §8.1.7 the §8.1.4 shape rather than the §8.1.2 shape: require `cr` to append a fixed, `cr`-owned citation block listing every resolved citation as `path:line` beneath the agent-written body at render time, outside the editable body and protected by §2.7 exactly as the question label is. Failing that, add the §8.1.5-style check: `cr post` MUST refuse, with exit code 1 naming the record id, to post a `cited` record whose body does not contain every one of its citations verbatim as `path:line`.

finding: §8.3.3 says "The **payload hash** MUST be the normalised hash of the comments array alone", but §1.4 defines normalisation over decoded text and its `normalised hash` over "the normalised text" — it says nothing about how a JSON array becomes that text. Field order, key order, escaping, and numeric formatting are all unfixed, and §1.4.4's collapsing of whitespace runs hides indentation but not ordering. The value must be reproducible across binary versions, because §8.4.4 requires `cr post --reconcile` to "list the PR's reviews, match the embedded payload hash of §8.4.3, and either adopt that review as posted or clear the state for a retry" — a hash that shifts between versions turns the double-post guard into a silent duplicate post, which §8.4.4 itself calls "a worse failure than posting late".
suggestion: Define the exact pre-image in §8.3.3: name the comment fields in a fixed order (for example `path`, `line`, `side`, `body`), state that each comment is serialised as those fields joined by LF, that comments are joined in payload order by LF, and that the resulting text is then normalised and hashed per §1.4.

finding: §8.4 covers exactly one network write: "The GitHub review-creation call is atomic: it either creates the review with all its comments or creates nothing." Two other writes were added or reinforced this round and fall outside it. §8.3.4 requires replies to be "posted into its existing thread rather than as a new review comment, in the same `cr post --confirm` invocation and after the review call" — n replies are n separate, non-atomic calls — and §9.5.3 adds a resolution comment that "MUST be written to the round's `posted.json`". If the third of five replies fails or times out, §8.4.2's "no state MUST be marked posted" is already false (the review succeeded), and §8.4.4's recovery cannot help: `--reconcile` matches "the embedded payload hash of §8.4.3", which §8.3.3 computes over "the comments array alone", so replies and resolutions are outside the hash and outside reconciliation. §9.5.3's promise that "no network write escapes the record" is unenforceable.
suggestion: Extend §8.4 to a per-write ledger: each reply and resolution is appended to `posted.json` with its own outcome (`pending`, `posted`, `failed`, `unknown`) before and after its call, and `cr post --reconcile` reconciles each pending or unknown entry by listing the thread's comments, not only the review's payload hash.

finding: §9.2.1 permits `LEFT` anchors — "`LEFT` anchors a removed line and MUST be used only for records about deletions" — but §9.2.2's migration procedure has no LEFT branch: "`cr` MUST scan the new file from line 1 for a window of `n` consecutive lines whose joined normalised hash equals the stored content hash". A LEFT anchor's stored content is by definition a line that does not exist in the head, so stage one finds zero matches in the new file and stage two's context window is drawn from the same removed region. §9.2.4 then sends it to `stale-anchor` on every head change, including a push that never touched the file. Since §9.2.2 says "every anchor of an open record MUST be re-resolved", every deletion finding decays to `stale-anchor` after the first push, and §10.2.4 then keeps a high-severity one blocking convergence indefinitely.
suggestion: Say which text a LEFT anchor is re-resolved against — the merge base of the new head, not the head — and apply the same two-stage window scan there. State that a LEFT anchor becomes stale only when the removed line reappears in the head or the merge base moves such that the line no longer exists in it.

finding: §9.4.1 copies §6.2's in-unit exclusion into the `fixed` bar, where its rationale inverts. It requires that "the outcome may be `fixed` only when at least one citation resolves against the new head and lies outside the record's own unit". The exclusion exists in §6.2 because a finding that cites the very line it complains about proves nothing (§6.2.5: "the in-unit exemption of the `cited` row would be self-granted"). For a verification the opposite holds: the evidence that a concern was addressed is normally the changed line at the anchor, i.e. inside the record's own unit. As written, the ordinary fix — author edits the flagged lines — can never be recorded `fixed`, and §9.4.1's own fallback forces it elsewhere: "Where the bar is not met the outcome MUST be recorded as `partial` instead", which per §9.4.2 creates a reply record posted into the author's thread. So every genuine fix produces an unnecessary comment on the author's PR implying the concern still stands, and §9.5.1 ("A record in any other state MUST be rejected with exit code 4") means the thread can never be resolved. Volume is itself a cost under §1.6, and this spends it on threads that are already closed in substance. Compounding it, "the record's own unit" is not well defined at the new head: §3.4.6 reuses a unit id only "for a unit whose file paths and hunk ranges are unchanged", and a fix changes them, so after the fix the record's stored `unit` names a unit that no longer exists in the current unit set and the outside-the-unit test has no referent.
suggestion: Drop the in-unit exclusion from §9.4.1 and state the bar in its own terms: `fixed` requires at least one citation that resolves against the new head and whose stored content hash differs from the one recorded at the time the finding was raised — i.e. the cited code demonstrably changed. Say explicitly that citing the record's own anchor is the expected case for a fix, and that the §6.2 exclusion does not carry over because its rationale is about self-supporting findings, not about verification. Also define the referent for any unit comparison at a new head, or remove the unit test entirely.

finding: §9.4.1 requires that `cr verify` accept "`--citation <path>:<line>`, repeatable, and `--probe <id>`" and that "`cr` MUST store the citations on the record with `origin: agent` and their computed hashes"; §9.4 and §9.6.2 also require the `--evidence <text>` to be stored on the record, and §9.5.2 requires "substituting the stored evidence and citations". The §6.1 record schema has no field for any of them. Writing them into the existing `citations` array is worse than a gap: §6.2.1 computes the grade from "`citations` and the referenced probe record", so the act of verifying a fix would silently promote an `argued` finding to `cited`, and §9.2.5 would then re-resolve verification citations as if they were the finding's own warrant.
suggestion: Add three computed fields to the §6.1 table — `verification_outcome`, `verification_evidence`, and `verification_citations` (same `{path, line, content_hash, origin}` shape) — state that they are written only by `cr verify` and `cr accept`, and state explicitly in §6.2.1 that they are not inputs to grading.

finding: §9.4.1's probe alternative uses "supports" in the one polarity the spec defines, and it is the wrong one. It permits `fixed` when "a same-head probe supports it". The only definition of a probe supporting anything is support for the finding: §6.2's `probed` row reads "whose result supports the claim per §5.3 and §5.4", §5.3.5 says "Only `no-test-failed` proves the gap", and §5.4.4 says "The probe MUST be treated as supporting the finding only when the finding's `claim` field names the claim the test asserts". Read against those, a mutation probe returning `no-test-failed` — the result that proves the test gap is still open — would authorise the `fixed` outcome, while the result that actually evidences a fix, `failed`, is the one §5.3.6 calls "disproves the gap" and is nowhere permitted to support `fixed`. Because §9.5.1 lets `cr resolve` close the thread of any record in `fixed`, and §9.5.2 then posts a `cr`-owned template "substituting the stored evidence and citations", the outcome is `cr` itself telling the author a concern was addressed on the strength of a probe result proving it was not. That is a false assertion, in `cr`'s own voice, in the one channel §9.5.2 was tightened to make trustworthy.
suggestion: Define fix-supporting probe results explicitly and separately from finding-supporting ones. For a mutation probe, the fix-supporting result is `failed` against the same filter that previously returned `no-test-failed`, with both probe ids stored on the record; for a gap probe it is `passed` where the earlier same-`claim` run was `failed`. State that `no-test-failed`, `no-tests-selected`, `inconclusive`, `error`, and `timeout` MUST NOT support `fixed`, mirroring §5.3.5, and never reuse the bare word "supports" in §9.4.1 without naming the direction.

finding: §9.4.2 says the reply record `cr` creates carries "`reply_to` with the original's `thread_id`, the original's `class`, `axis`, `unit`, and `anchor`, and `kind: question`", and §9.6.5 queues a withdrawal reply "as a reply record per §9.4.2". §6.1 marks `role`, `severity`, `summary`, and `evidence` as Required = yes and `grade` as computed, and §6.1.3 makes `cr merge` and `cr record` "reject a record missing any field marked required, with exit code 1". Nothing says what those four fields hold on a `cr`-generated reply, and §8.1.2 forbids `cr` from composing prose while §7.2.3 says a block that carries no role, axis, or `cr`-computed grade cannot enter the corpus. A tester cannot assert the contents of the record, its grade, or whether §8.1.5's "no `?` character" check applies to it.
suggestion: Enumerate the reply record fully in §9.4.2: inherit `role` and `severity` from the original, set `grade` to the recomputed value, and define `summary`/`evidence` as `cr`-owned template text (protected like the §9.5.2 resolution template, so §8.1.2 is not violated) — or exempt reply records from the required-field check in §6.1.3 by name.

finding: §9.5.2's repair contradicts itself and leaves the second prose channel open. It says "`cr resolve` MUST NOT post agent-composed prose: it MUST post a built-in, `cr`-owned template for `render.lang`, naming the record id and substituting the stored evidence and citations" — but the stored evidence is exactly agent-composed prose: §9.4 requires the agent to record the outcome "through `cr verify <pr> <id> --outcome <outcome> --evidence <text>`". The template frames agent text; it does not replace it. That text reaches the author without passing the read-before-send step every other posted body passes: §8.1.2 states "Editing the draft is the only input path for reader-facing prose: `cr` MUST NOT translate or compose, and MUST NOT accept a body through any other channel", yet `--evidence` is precisely such a channel, and no §7.1 draft block ever renders it for the human to edit. The `--confirm` on `cr resolve` does not substitute: §8.5.1's dry-run obligation to "print the full payload" is scoped to `cr post` and has no §9.5 counterpart, so the reviewer confirms a body they have not been shown. It is also in the wrong language by construction — §6.1.1 stores `evidence` in English while the template is rendered for `render.lang`.
suggestion: Route the resolution comment through the draft like every other posted body: have `cr verify --outcome fixed` queue a resolution block into the next draft, rendered from the template with the evidence substituted, and let `cr resolve --confirm` post only what the human left in that block. If a separate command is kept, add a §8.5.1 counterpart to §9.5 requiring `cr resolve` without `--confirm` to print the exact body it would post and report `"posted": false`, and delete or rewrite the clause "MUST NOT post agent-composed prose", which the same sentence contradicts.

finding: §9.1's transition table lists "| `awaiting-author`, `answered`, `regressed`, `stale-anchor` | `accepted` | `cr accept` |", but §9.6.1 says acceptance "MUST apply only to a record in `awaiting-author`, `answered`, or `stale-anchor`, and MUST reject any other state with exit code 4". `regressed` is permitted by one and rejected by the other. This is not cosmetic: §9.1 lists no other exit from `regressed` except `verifying` via `cr recheck`, and §10.2.4 says an open `regressed` record at severity high blocks convergence, so under §9.6.1 a regressed record that the reviewer wants to drop has no terminal path at all.
suggestion: Pick one. If `regressed` may be accepted, add it to §9.6.1's list; if not, delete it from the §9.1 row and say in §9.6 why a regressed original must be re-verified rather than withdrawn.

finding: §9.1's transition table lists "| `awaiting-author`, `answered`, `regressed`, `stale-anchor` | `accepted` | `cr accept` |", while §9.6.1 says accept "MUST apply only to a record in `awaiting-author`, `answered`, or `stale-anchor`, and MUST reject any other state with exit code 4". `regressed` is permitted by one and rejected by the other, and §9.1's "Transitions are exhaustive. A transition not listed here MUST be rejected with exit code 4" gives no precedence rule. The test "`cr accept` on a record in state `regressed`" is written as exit 0 by one engineer and exit 4 by the other.
suggestion: Decide whether a regressed concern may be withdrawn and make both statements agree — either add `regressed` to §9.6.1's list or drop it from the §9.1 row — and state that §9.1's table is the normative source when a per-command section enumerates states.

finding: §9.1's transition table permits `cr accept` from `regressed` — "| `awaiting-author`, `answered`, `regressed`, `stale-anchor` | `accepted` | `cr accept` |" — while §9.6.1 forbids exactly that: "It MUST apply only to a record in `awaiting-author`, `answered`, or `stale-anchor`, and MUST reject any other state with exit code 4." Both are MUSTs about the same command and the same state, and §9.1 additionally declares "Transitions are exhaustive. A transition not listed here MUST be rejected with exit code 4", so the table is normative too. An implementer must guess which of the two guards to code.
suggestion: Pick one and make the other match. `regressed` already has an exit through `cr recheck` → `verifying`, so the conservative repair is to drop `regressed` from the §9.1 accept row; otherwise add `regressed` to §9.6.1's permitted list.

finding: §9.6.1 permits accepting a record in `stale-anchor`, and §9.6.5 then requires that "Accepting MUST queue a withdrawal reply into the next draft, as a reply record per §9.4.2" — and §9.4.2 builds that reply from "the original's `class`, `axis`, `unit`, and `anchor`". A `stale-anchor` record is by §9.1 one whose "anchor no longer resolves after a force-push", yet §6.1.2 requires that "Every record MUST carry an anchor that resolves to a line in the current head" and §7.2's marker table aborts when "the anchor no longer resolves". So the withdrawal reply that §9.6.5 mandates for a stale-anchor acceptance is a record the spec forbids recording and forbids drafting — the single case where §9.6.5 matters most (the author cannot even see the anchor any more) is the case it cannot execute.
suggestion: State that a reply record inherits `reply_to` and posts into an existing thread, and is therefore exempt from §6.1.2's resolving-anchor requirement and from the §7.2 anchor re-validation — the thread id, not the anchor, is what locates it. Alternatively require the reply to carry no anchor at all and say explicitly that §1.6.1 does not apply because it is not a new anchored comment.

finding: §9.6.5 requires a withdrawal reply "as a reply record per §9.4.2", and §9.4.2 fixes that record's shape as "`kind: question`". Two render rules then fire on it. §8.1.4: `cr` "MUST prepend a fixed, `cr`-owned label line to every `kind=question` comment, naming the register and the grade", and §8.1.5: `cr` "MUST refuse to post a `kind=question` body containing no `?` character, with exit code 1". So the comment that says "I am no longer asking about this" is stamped with the question register and cannot be posted unless it is phrased as a question. §9.6.5's own rationale is that "the thread still reads as an open objection" — the mandated rendering guarantees it still does.
suggestion: Give the reply record a `reply_kind` of `question` or `withdrawal` (and `partial` for §9.4.2's case), exempt `withdrawal` from §8.1.5's `?` requirement, and have §8.1.4 prepend a distinct built-in withdrawal label. §6.3's forcing is unaffected because a withdrawal asserts nothing about the code.

finding: §9.6.5 requires that "Accepting MUST queue a withdrawal reply into the next draft, as a reply record per §9.4.2 carrying `reply_to` with the record's `thread_id`", and §9.6.1 permits accepting a record in `stale-anchor`. But §9.1's table reaches `stale-anchor` from `draft` and `queued` — "| `draft`, `queued`, `awaiting-author`, `answered`, `verifying`, `regressed` | `stale-anchor` | `cr recheck` |" — and such a record was never posted, so `thread_id` (§6.1: "GitHub thread id once posted") is absent. The mandated reply then has no thread to reply into, and §8.3.4 requires a reply record to be "posted into its existing thread rather than as a new review comment", which does not exist. The §9.6 preamble also calls the subject "a posted concern", contradicting the admission of never-posted records.
suggestion: Restrict §9.6.1 to records that carry a `thread_id`, rejecting an unposted record with exit code 4 and pointing the reviewer at plain discard per §7.2; or make §9.6.5 conditional — "queue a withdrawal reply only when the record carries a `thread_id`" — and say what happens to an unposted accepted record instead.

finding: §9.6.5's withdrawal reply cannot be posted, so the harm the repair names — "A concern the reviewer has silently dropped is worse than one never raised: the author is still working against it, and the thread still reads as an open objection" — survives the repair. It requires the withdrawal to be queued "as a reply record per §9.4.2", and §9.4.2 fixes such a record at "`kind: question`". §8.1.5 then blocks it: "`cr` MUST refuse to post a `kind=question` body containing no `?` character, with exit code 1 naming the record id." A withdrawal is a statement, not a question, so the natural body fails the check, and because §8.3.4 posts replies "in the same `cr post --confirm` invocation", the exit-1 refusal takes the whole round down with it. There is no escape hatch: §7.2's marker table permits `question`→`finding` "only when the recomputed grade is `probed` or `cited`", and a reply record carries no citations and no probe, so it is `argued` and §6.3.1 forces it back to a question anyway. A second, narrower block hits the same path: §9.6.1 permits accepting a record in `stale-anchor`, but §9.4.2 clones "the original's ... `anchor`", and §6.1.2 demands "an anchor that resolves to a line in the current head", which by definition a stale anchor does not — even though a reply posted into an existing thread needs no line anchor at all.
suggestion: Give withdrawal replies their own record shape rather than reusing §9.4.2's. Exempt records carrying `reply_to` from §8.1.5's question-mark check and from §6.3.1's forcing, since they are posted into an existing thread and assert nothing new, or introduce a third `kind` (e.g. `reply`) that §8.1.4 labels with its own `cr`-owned line. Likewise exempt `reply_to` records from §6.1.2's resolving-anchor requirement, stating that a thread reply is located by `thread_id` and needs no anchor, so a `stale-anchor` record accepted under §9.6.1 can still have its withdrawal delivered.

finding: §2.6.1 makes built-in rules the bottom resolution layer — "Rules MUST resolve in layers, highest first: per-repository, then global, then the profile's built-in rules" — but nothing defines that layer. The §2.4 profile schema has no rules field, §2.2 lists only `~/.cr/rules/<id>.json` and the per-repository directory, and §11 says `cr init` writes "default profiles and roles" with no mention of rules. An implementer has no way to know whether `laravel-pest` and `generic` are required to carry rules, what they are, or where they are read from.
suggestion: Either add a `rules` array (rule objects or ids) to the §2.4 profile schema and state which rules the two shipped profiles carry, or delete the third layer from §2.6.1 and state that v0.1 ships no built-in rules, so the corpus starts empty and grows through §2.6.3.

finding: §3.4.6 keys unit identity on position — the `id` is "stable for the life of the PR and reused across rounds for a unit whose file paths and hunk ranges are unchanged" — while §10.2.2 keys coverage carry-over on content: "A unit unchanged since an earlier round keeps its cells ... a unit whose content changed needs its row filled again." Any edit earlier in the same file shifts a later unit's hunk ranges without touching its lines, so its `id` is not reused even though its unit hash is identical. Cells are keyed by unit id per §4.5.5, so the carry-over §10.2.2 promises cannot be looked up, and the untouched unit's whole row must be refilled. §9.2 defines migration for anchors in exactly this situation but nothing migrates a unit id.
suggestion: Key unit id reuse on the unit hash rather than on hunk ranges: reuse the `id` of the prior round's unit with the same file paths and the same unit hash, allowing its ranges to move, and reserve a fresh `id` for units whose hash changed. State that a reused id keeps its cells per §10.2.2.

finding: §4.3.1 requires `cr` to "search the repository for candidate pre-existing symbols", and §4.3.2 then pins an exact ranking and an exact cap — "ordered by similarity descending, then path ascending, then line ascending, and `cr` MUST attach at most `reinvention.max_candidates` (default 5)". The candidate pool itself is never bounded: nothing says whether the symbol index honours `ignore.globs` (which §3.4.2 applies to the diff only), excludes vendored or generated trees, excludes test files, or is limited to `match.globs`. Since the cap truncates a ranked list, the pool determines which five candidates the agent sees, so a fixture test on the attached candidate list has no determinate expected value.
suggestion: State the pool explicitly in §4.3.1: symbols declared in files matching the profile's `match.globs`, excluding `ignore.globs` and the files changed by the diff, at the merge base.

finding: §5.3.4's ladder "is total over every run — no run can match two rungs, and none can match none" and §5.4.3's is "total over every run", yet §5.1.7 says "A probe whose post-run cleanliness check fails MUST be recorded with result `error`" — an outcome decided after the ladder has already assigned one. No precedence is stated. For the observable case "mutation applied, no test failed, probe artefact left behind" one engineer records `no-test-failed` (the ladder is total) and the other records `error` (§5.1.7 is a MUST), and only the second one blocks the `probed` grade.
suggestion: Add the cleanliness failure as rung 0 of both ladders, or state in §5.1.7 that its `error` result overrides the rung selected by §5.3.4/§5.4.3 and amend the totality sentences to say the ladder is total over runs that pass the post-run check.

finding: The marker-semantics table requires a triage event for a severity edit — "| `severity` | Freely editable; recorded as a triage event |" — and the verb table requires one for softening. But §7.3.1 closes the vocabulary: events are keyed by "(PR, round, record id, action)", `cr post --confirm` writes "exactly one outcome event per queued record, drawn from `kept`, `softened`, `discarded-not-here`, and `discarded-wrong`", and "These five action names are the complete vocabulary the statistics below are computed from." There is no action name a severity edit can use, and the exactly-one-outcome-per-record rule leaves no room for a second event on the same record.
suggestion: Either drop "recorded as a triage event" from the `severity` row and record the severity change on the record alone, or add a sixth action name (for example `reseverity`) to §7.3.1, state that it is not an outcome event so the exactly-one rule is unaffected, and say explicitly that §7.3.3's demotion rate ignores it.

finding: §7.1.1 puts only `path` and `line` in the marker, and §7.2's table makes them editable: "Re-validated against the current head; aborts when the anchor no longer resolves". But §9.2 defines an anchor as carrying "`path`, `side`, `start_line`, `line`, a normalised content hash, and up to three lines of context on each side", and nothing says any of those are recomputed when the user edits the marker. Two consequences follow. A multi-line anchor cannot be expressed in the marker at all, so editing `line` alone silently breaks the `start_line` ≤ `line` relation the content hash was computed over. And after the edit the record carries a content hash for the old lines, which §9.2.2 will use next round to migrate the anchor straight back to where the user moved it away from, and which §7.4.1 will use as the "normalised hash of the anchored lines" in any waiver key.
suggestion: State that a marker edit to `path` or `line` makes `cr` recompute the whole anchor object — `start_line` set equal to the new `line` unless the marker also carries `start_line`, plus a fresh content hash and context — and record the retarget as a triage event. Add `start_line` to the §7.1.1 marker fields so a multi-line anchor is editable at all.

finding: §7.2's marker table says of `severity`: "Freely editable; recorded as a triage event", but §7.3.1 closes the action vocabulary — "drawn from `kept`, `softened`, `discarded-not-here`, and `discarded-wrong`" plus `raised`, and "These five action names are the complete vocabulary". A severity edit has no action name, and §7.3.1 keys events by `(PR, round, record id, action)`, so the mandated event cannot be written or asserted on. A tester cannot decide whether editing severity produces a sixth action, overwrites the `raised` event, or produces nothing.
suggestion: Either add a sixth action name (e.g. `reseverity`, carrying the old and new values) and say explicitly that it is excluded from the §7.3.3 statistics, or drop "recorded as a triage event" from the §7.2 `severity` row and record the change in `transitions.ndjson` instead.

finding: §7.4.8 specifies "`cr waivers remove <id> --repo <owner/repo> [--pr <number>]` MUST delete one from either scope", but no waiver `id` is ever defined. §7.4.1 says a waiver "MUST be keyed by `(anchor.path, class, rule id when present, normalised hash of the anchored lines)`" and §7.4.9 adds round, PR, head, and reason — no identifier field, no format, and no statement that the id is stable across rounds, which removal by id requires.
suggestion: Add an `id` field to §7.4: define it as a short deterministic value derived from the §7.4.1 key (for example the first 12 hex characters of the normalised hash of the key's joined components), state that it is computed by `cr` and stable while the key is, and require `cr waivers list` to print it.

finding: §8.3.1 says "All comments in a round MUST be posted as one GitHub review" and §8.4.3 says `cr` "MUST embed the payload hash as an HTML comment in the review's own body before posting", while §8.3.4 posts replies "in the same `cr post --confirm` invocation and after the review call". A round produced solely by §9.6.5 acceptance withdrawals or §9.4.2 partial replies has zero new comments, and the spec never says whether `cr` still creates a review — an empty-comment review purely to carry the payload hash — or skips the review call and posts only the replies. The choice is observable: it determines whether the author gets a notification, whether `rounds/<n>/posted.json` has a payload hash at all, and whether §10.3's mandated "payload hash of §8.3.3" exists for the round.
suggestion: State that `cr` creates the review only when the round queues at least one anchored comment; that a reply-only round posts replies alone, records `payload_hash: null` in `posted.json` and in §10.3's summary, and is reconciled by the per-thread procedure rather than by payload hash.

finding: §8.3.4 opens a second network-write channel with none of the protections §8.4 gives the first. It requires replies to be "posted into its existing thread rather than as a new review comment, in the same `cr post --confirm` invocation and after the review call", but §8.4's guarantees are all scoped to the review call: §8.4.1 "The GitHub review-creation call is atomic", §8.4.2 "If the call is rejected, no state MUST be marked posted", and §8.4.4's recovery, which "MUST list the PR's reviews, match the embedded payload hash of §8.4.3". Replies are not reviews and carry no embedded hash, so a run that posts the review and then fails partway through its replies has no defined state and no reconciliation path; §8.3.3's payload hash is explicitly "the normalised hash of the comments array alone" and says nothing about replies. A retry after such a failure re-posts the replies that already landed, which is the outcome §8.4.4 calls out as the worse one: "Posting twice is a worse failure than posting late."
suggestion: Extend §8.4 to the reply channel: require each reply's outcome to be recorded in `posted.json` individually as it returns, define a `post-unresolved` state for replies as §8.4.4 does for the review, and make `cr post --reconcile` match already-posted replies by listing the thread's comments and comparing the normalised hash of each reply body before re-posting. State that a reply already present in its thread MUST be adopted, never re-sent.

finding: The §9.1 transition table and §9.6.1 disagree about accepting a `regressed` record, and both are normative and both are absolute. §9.1's table lists "| `awaiting-author`, `answered`, `regressed`, `stale-anchor` | `accepted` | `cr accept` |" under the heading "Transitions are exhaustive. A transition not listed here MUST be rejected with exit code 4", while §9.6.1 says `cr accept` "MUST apply only to a record in `awaiting-author`, `answered`, or `stale-anchor`, and MUST reject any other state with exit code 4". The two clauses give opposite answers for the same input, so conformance is undecidable and two implementations will differ on whether a reviewer can withdraw a concern that regressed. The mismatch is a by-product of this round's change, which added `regressed` as a transition source in three table rows without revisiting §9.6.1.
suggestion: Pick one and make the other follow. Since a regressed concern is still open and still on the author's screen, allowing withdrawal is the more useful reading; if so, add `regressed` to §9.6.1's list. If not, remove it from the `accepted` row of §9.1's table. Either way state the reason inline so the next edit to one does not silently desynchronise the other.

finding: Two §11 rows drop a flag their defining section makes mandatory. §3.6.1 specifies `cr note <ISSUE-KEY> "<text>" --source <source>` and §3.6.3 closes the vocabulary — "Valid sources MUST be `chat`, `jira`, `thread`, `meeting`, and `other`" — but the §11 rows read `cr note <ISSUE-KEY> <text>` and `cr answer <pr> <question-id> <text>`, while §3.6.2 specifies `cr answer <pr> <question-id> "<text>" --source <source>`. §11 is the table an implementer builds the CLI surface from, and a note stored without a source cannot satisfy §3.6.5's requirement that `cr context` "print the accumulated notes with provenance".
suggestion: Add `--source <source>` to both §11 rows, and state whether it is required or defaults to `other`.

finding: The `reply_to` row reads "Thread id this record replies to, set by `cr verify --outcome partial` (§9.4.2)", naming a single producer. §9.6.5 adds a second — a withdrawal reply "carrying `reply_to` with the record's `thread_id`" — and §9.1's transition table already lists both: "— (new reply record) | `draft` | `cr verify --outcome partial` (§9.4.2), `cr accept` (§9.6.5)". The schema table is the one place an implementer reads to learn who may write a field.
suggestion: Change the row to "set by `cr verify --outcome partial` (§9.4.2) and `cr accept` (§9.6.5)", matching the §9.1 row.

finding: §7.3.1's repair closes the action vocabulary at five names while §7.2 still mandates a sixth event with no name. §7.3.1 ends "These five action names are the complete vocabulary the statistics below are computed from", enumerating `raised`, `kept`, `softened`, `discarded-not-here`, and `discarded-wrong`. But §7.2's marker table requires an event for a severity edit — "| `severity` | Freely editable; recorded as a triage event |" — and none of the five names covers it, so either the event is unrepresentable or the vocabulary is not complete. Since §7.3.1 also keys events by `(PR, round, record id, action)`, an unnamed action has no key and cannot be written idempotently.
suggestion: Either add a sixth action name (e.g. `reseverity`, carrying the old and new severity) to §7.3.1's enumeration and say it is excluded from the §7.3.3 demotion rate, or amend §7.2's `severity` row to say the edit is applied but not recorded as a triage event, so the vocabulary claim in §7.3.1 stays true.
